title: Precision engineering chiral interfaces for efficient spin injection in metal halide heterostructures

paper_content.abstract: Precise control of interfaces is crucial for spin generation, transport, and detection in opto-spintronics. However, the interface engineering for efficient spin injection remains a significant challenge. Here, we synthesized a helical structure of PbI2 (R-PbI2) via an interfacial chirality-induced growth approach at the heterostructure interface. This few-nanometer-thick R-PbI2 layer shows a lower lattice mismatch with both the adjacent R-NEAPbI3 (R-NEA refers to R-1-(1-naphtyl)ethylamine) and PbI2 layers, and leads to an optimal chiral interface in the chiral heterostructure with minimized residual strain and defect density. Combined with circularly polarized pump-probe spectroscopic and spin-photovoltaic measurements, our chiral heterostructure interface contributes a spin-injection efficiency up to 68%, thus leading to a degree of polarization of 29% in photocurrent. The precise synthesis of a chiral interface offers a promising route to manipulate spin dynamics and achieve a high degree of spin polarization required for advanced opto-spintronic applications.
paper_content.introduction:
The generation of spin-polarized charge carriers in semiconductors is the fundamental prerequisite for opto-spintronics1–3. Major approaches for generating spin-polarized carriers rely on spin injection by ferromagnetic contact or circularly polarized light4,5, but typically require cryogenic temperatures, external magnetic fields, or precise optical alignment. Recently, chiral metal halide semiconductors (MHSs) have emerged as promising materials in opto-spintronics due to their strong spin-orbit coupling and chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS)6–9, enabling room-temperature spin polarization without external magnetic fields. However, insulating chiral organic components lead to relatively poor charge transport and electron-phonon spin depolarization, which limits their performance10,11. Heterostructures that consist of chiral MHSs and achiral semiconductors have been demonstrated to enhance the charge transport and the degree of polarization12–16. This approach synergistically combines the spin selectivity of chiral MHSs with the optoelectronic properties of achiral semiconductors17–19.

The interface plays a critical role in both optoelectronic and spintronic applications. In optoelectronics, its precise characteristics control charge separation and recombination, directly impacting performance. For spintronics, the interface is crucial for the effective injection, manipulation, and detection of spin-polarized carriers. Therefore, the selection of a robust fabrication method for the heterostructure is essential. Previous heterostructure fabrication methods include dry-transfer stacking18, hot-casting14, solution-based spin-coating20, and self-assembly21. The interfacial characteristics in terms of morphology, defect density, bonding, and chemical interaction in chiral MHS heterostructures can govern their functional properties, particularly charge transfer, spin dynamics, and chiroptical responses. Dry-transfer method generally aims for chemically inert interfaces to preserve the integrity of the constituent layers18. Hot-casting method relies on specific and designed chemical bonds14. Spin-coating and self-assembly methods can involve interfacial chemical transformations, which might be leveraged for in-situ tuning of properties but also pose challenges in predictability20,21.

Here, we synthesize chiral MHS heterostructures by an interfacial chirality-induced growth approach with PbI2 and R-NEAI (R-NEA denotes R-1-(1-naphtyl)ethylamine) solutions. The chiral interface is engineered with a high-crystallinity and helical R-PbI2 layer, which effectively suppresses interfacial spin depolarization and leads to a spin-injection efficiency of up to 68%. Our results demonstrate that lattice mismatch, residual strain, and defect density at the interface are critical factors for spin-injection efficiency. A spin-photovoltaic device of R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure achieves 29% degree of polarization in photocurrent, twice that of previously reported chiral MHS heterostructures15,16. This chiral MHS heterostructure growth approach paves the way for efficient spin injection and a high degree of spin polarization at room temperature, advancing the development of opto-spintronic applications.
paper_content.results:
Synthesis of the chiral interface by an interfacial chirality-induced growth method
We spin-coated a precursor solution containing equimolar amounts of PbI2 and R-NEAI onto a glass substrate, followed by annealing at 100 °C for 5 min to grow the R-NEAPbI3 film. Subsequently, the film was post-annealed at 100 °C in air to in-situ grow the PbI2 layer on the top of R-NEAPbI3 (details are provided in the Method). The delocalized R-NEA+ cations between R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 induced a chiral lattice deformation of PbI2 by interfacial chirality transfer22, shown in Fig. 1a. In the post-annealing process, the R-NEAPbI3 is mainly converted into PbI2, with only a small amount of conversion to a few-nanometer-thickness R-PbI2 between R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2. The R-NEAPbI3 phase content decreased with increasing annealing time, while the PbI2 content correspondingly increased. From the in-situ X-ray diffraction spectra in Fig. 1b, the peak at 12.7° refers to the (001) peak of the PbI2 phase and becomes prominent with increasing annealing time. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the (002) peak of the R-NEAPbI3 phase slightly increases from 0.16° to 0.18° with the annealing time. The increase in FWHM of the (002) peak of R-NEAPbI3 is mainly due to the precipitation of PbI2, which reduces the grain size of the remaining R-NEAPbI3 domains, as estimated from the Scherrer equation23. The in-situ X-ray diffraction spectra show that there is no by-product (R-NEA)2PbI4, whose diffraction peak of the (002) plane is at 5.8° (Figure S1). The PbI2 content can be estimated by the energy-dispersive X-ray spectra shown in Figure S2. We achieved 6% PbI2 after 30 min of post-annealing.

In Fig. 1c, as the post-annealing time increases, R-NEAPbI3 is partially converted into PbI2, evidenced by the weakening of the R-NEAPbI3 absorption peak24 at 375 nm and the strengthening of the PbI2 absorption peak25 at 500 nm (detailed analysis in Figure S3). In Fig. 1d, a pair of reverse circular dichroism (CD) peaks at 376 nm and 408 nm corresponds to the excitonic absorption of R-NEAPbI3. Additionally, shoulders near 500 nm in CD spectra are caused by the excitonic absorption of PbI2 rather than (R-NEA)2PbI4. These shoulders become more pronounced with increasing PbI2 content, suggesting that the PbI2 lattice undergoes chiral deformation. The absorption dissymmetry factor, gCD, at 500 nm reaches a maximum value of 0.02 at a PbI2 concentration of 6% (Figure S4). Consequently, CHS-I at this concentration was selected for subsequent research, as it yielded R-PbI2 with the highest relative proportion of PbI2.

A comparable CD spectral feature appears in the S-configuration samples, though with reversed polarity (Figure S5). In contrast, the racemic sample exhibits no CD response (Figure S5). To distinguish the true CD signal from artifacts arising from linear circular dichroism and linear birefringence, we extracted the genuine CD signal following established methods26 (detailed analysis in Supplementary Information). This genuine signal persists at 500 nm corresponds to the exciton absorption peak of PbI2, indicating that the shoulder peak at this wavelength originates from the intrinsic chirality of R-PbI2 rather than experimental artifacts. To assess the universality of this interfacial chirality-induced growth method, we performed post-annealing treatments on 1D R-MBAPbI3, 2D (R-MBA)2PbI4, and 2D (R-4-Br-MBA)2PbI4 (where R-MBA and R-4-Br-MBA denote R-1-phenylethanamine and R-1-(4-bromophenyl)ethanamine, respectively). In these films, the CD signal near 500 nm increases significantly with extended post-annealing time, a trend attributed to the formation of R-PbI2 (Figure S6).

This lattice distortion is further supported by our DFT calculations (details in Supplementary Information and Figure S7). The deformation is attributed to asymmetric hydrogen bonding (H2N–H···I) between the iodine atoms of PbI2 and R-NEA+ at the interface, which induces structure distortion in PbI2 and leads to the formation of a chiral R-PbI2 layer. The chiral axis of R-PbI2 is parallel to the in-plane direction of R-NEAPbI3. From the atomic force microscopic image in Fig. 1e, PbI2 grown on top of the R-NEAPbI3 shows a flake-like structure and inserted vertically into the R-NEAPbI3 layer. The PbI2 flakes have a length of 1.2±0.3 μm, a width of 39±8 nm, and a thickness of 145±0.5 nm. The size and distribution of PbI2 flakes can be tuned by changing the post-annealing time (see Figure S8 for more details).

We characterized the lattice structure using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) in Fig. 1f. The image reveals two distinct lattice structures in the heterostructure, a lattice spacing of 0.362 nm, corresponding to the (013) plane of R-NEAPbI3, and a lattice spacing of 0.338 nm and 0.348 nm, associated with the (002) plane of PbI2 and R-PbI2, respectively. Using Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms, we isolated the (002) plane of PbI2 at the interface by applying a mask. Within a 5 nm-thick region at the interface, detailed analysis reveals a helical lattice distortion featuring a spiral radius of 0.02 nm and a pitch of 0.84 nm. These observations agree with our DFT calculations. The interface exhibits chirality because the helically arranged R-NEA+ cations transfer their chiral information to the adjacent PbI2, inducing a helical structure in the PbI2.

Chiral heterostructure interface characterizations
Two different chiral MHS heterostructures are synthesized to demonstrate the critical role of the R-PbI2 layer at the interface. CHS-I refers to the heterostructure with R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 and R-PbI2/PbI2 interfaces, and CHS-II refers to the heterostructure with only R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 interface. CHS-II is synthesized without interfacial chirality-induced growth, resulting in PbI2 forming nanoparticles with a diameter of 150±20 nm. The PbI2 nanoparticles is embedded within R-NEAPbI3 layer, as shown in Figure S9. CD response and gCD are zero at 500 nm regardless of the PbI2 content27 (Figure S10), indicating the absence of helical lattice distortion in PbI2 of CHS-II.

In Fig. 2a, we plot the schematic lattice structures of both CHS-I and CHS-II. In CHS-II, the lattice mismatch is mainly located at the R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 interface, whereas in CHS-I, it is primarily at the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 interface. HR-TEM analysis in Fig. 1f reveals that the R-NEAPbI3 (103) plane contacts the PbI2 or R-PbI2 (002) plane, with lattice fringes intersecting at approximately 65°. We calculated the interfacial lattice mismatch28 using the measured interplanar spacings, d(103)=0.362 nm for R-NEAPbI3, d(002)=0.338 nm for PbI2, and d'(002)=0.348 nm for R-PbI2. This yields a lattice mismatch of 3.9% for CHS-I and 6.6% for CHS-II. The lower lattice mismatch in CHS-I shows that the R-PbI2 interlayer effectively relieves the interfacial lattice mismatch. Then we used grazing incident X-ray diffraction spectra shown in Figure S11 and related 2θ vs sin2φ plot in Fig. 2b to characterize the residual strain distribution in CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ. The tensile strain is determined from the slope of 2θ vs sin2φ plot29,30, yielding 0.42% for CHS-I and 1.48% for CHS-II. This reduced tensile strain in CHS-I is attributed to the flexibility of the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 interface31.

The defect densities of CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ were evaluated using the space-charge-limited current method (device configurations are in Figure S12), as shown in Fig. 2c,d. The current (I) initially increases linearly with voltage (V), which is the ohmic response. Then the current rises exponentially (I/Vn, n>2) at 0.14 V for CHS-I and 0.4 V for CHS-II, indicating a transition to the trap-filled limit (TFL), in which all the available trap (defect) states are filled by the injected carriers32. The onset voltage is determined by:

VTFL = en d L2 / 2εrε0 (1)

where L is film thickness, εr is the permittivity, and ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, and nd is the defect density33,34. Notably, nd in CHS-I is 0.39×1016 cm-3, approximately one-third that of CHS-II (1.10×1016 cm-3). To exclude sample-to-sample variability as the cause of the reduced defect density, we fabricated multiple devices for both CHS-I and CHS-II under identical synthesis and processing conditions (Figure S13). The nd of CHS-I is (0.38±0.04)×1016 cm-3, which is lower than that of CHS-II [(1.26±0.59)×1016 cm-3], indicating that CHS-I possesses a more efficient passivation mechanism than CHS-II. For CHS-I, post-annealing partially decomposes R-NEAPbI3 into PbI2 and R-NEAI, enriching the interface with excess R-NEA+ and I-. The R-NEA+ cations act as Lewis bases to passivate undercoordinated Pb and Pb vacancies, while I- compensates iodide vacancies, thereby reducing the interfacial defect density35.

To investigate the exciton dynamics in the heterostructure, we performed transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy using a linearly polarized pump pulse of 365 nm wavelength and a broadband linearly polarized probe. Figure 2e,f show the absorption difference between pump and probe (ΔA = Apump on - Apump off) from TA spectra. Figure 2e exhibits distinct ground state bleaching (GSB) signals at 410 nm and 500 nm for R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2, respectively. There are two photo-induced absorption signals at 450 nm and 520 nm for R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2, respectively. It indicates that excitons are formed after photo-excitation of R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 in the heterostructure. Figure 2f shows the time evolution of excitons probed in the GSB region at 500 nm. The TA signals exhibit mono-exponential decay kinetics, yielding an exciton lifetime of 16.9±0.3 ps for CHS-Ⅰ, which is longer than the 8.3±0.3 ps measured for CHS-Ⅱ. The exciton lifetime in CHS-I or CHS-II is shorter compared to that of pristine PbI2 (26.2±0.9 ps, Figure S14) due to promoted exciton dissociation in the type-II heterojunction formed by R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 heterostructure21. The shorter exciton lifetime in CHS-II (Fig. 2f) indicates more efficient exciton dissociation and charge transfer, consistent with the bulk heterostructure formed by PbI2 nanoparticles distributed throughout the R-NEAPbI3 matrix36. In contrast, the PbI2 nanosheets, vertically inserted R-NEAPbI3 matrix in CHS-I, provide a smaller interfacial area, leading to slower exciton dissociation and a longer lifetime.

Modulation of exciton spin dynamics at the chiral interface
We investigated the exciton spin polarization dynamics in the heterostructures at room temperature using circularly polarized TA (CTA) spectroscopy (schematic in Fig. 3a). A right-circularly polarized (σ+) pump pulse at 365 nm selectively generated excitons with angular momentum J=+1 in both PbI2 phase and R-NEAPbI3 phase. The exciton spin relaxation of this initial +1 state can lead to the formation of -1 exciton via spin-flip37. The subsequent dynamics were monitored by probing the TA spectra with broadband right- or left-circularly polarized light (σ+ or σ-). The time evolution of TA spectra collected at 500 nm with co-circular (σ+σ+) and cross-circular (σ+σ-) pump-probe configurations are shown in Fig. 3b,c. The relaxation of exciton spin polarization is evaluated by the difference between the TA signals obtained with co-circular and cross-circular configurations (ΔAσ+σ- - ΔAσ+σ+). Exponential fitting of the decay curves yields exciton spin relaxation times of 19.2±1.9 ps for the PbI2 phase in CHS-Ⅰ and 9.2±1.5 ps in CHS-Ⅱ, respectively. Based on temperature-dependent and pump fluence-dependent spin relaxation time, we determine that the spin relaxation in PbI2 is dominated by the Elliott-Yafet mechanism (details in Figure S15 and Figure S16). The spin relaxation time and bandgap of PbI2 are positively correlated38,

τE ∝ 1 / (E - Δso)2 E T2 τp (2)

where Δso is the spin-orbit splitting of the valence band, Eg is bandgap, T is temperature, τp is momentum relaxation time. A 0.06 eV bandgap increase in CHS-I (Figure S17) arises mainly from the PbI2 morphology rather than the few-nanometer R-PbI2 layer. The thickness of PbI2 in CHS-I (39±8 nm) is much thinner than that of CHS-II (150±20 nm), leading to stronger quantum confinement and thus a larger bandgap39, which in turn prolongs the exciton spin relaxation time in the PbI2 phase of CHS-I. The exciton lifetime τ and spin relaxation time τs determine the fraction of spin-polarized electrons before the spin injection at the interface, that is, a renormalization factor12:

F = 1 / (1 + τ / τs) (3)

The renormalization factors F for CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ are 53.2±2.5% and 52.6±4.2%, respectively, indicating that the initial spin polarization created by the light within the PbI2 layer is comparable for both samples. In contrast to typical TA spectra, where circularly polarized excitation directly induces spin polarization, the observed spin splitting between σ+ and σ- probe spectra under linearly polarized excitation must arise from the spin-selective electron transfer at the heterojunction (schematic in Fig. 3d). The excitation wavelength of linearly polarized pump pulse is fixed at 465 nm rather than 500 nm to selectively excite PbI2 phase and avoid the interference between the R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 excitons in the GSB region (500 nm), respectively. We measured the TA spectra with linear pump and σ+ or σ- probe, which are plotted in Fig. 3e,f. The degree of CTA polarization in PbI2 represents the degree of spin polarization between excitons with J=+1 and J=−1, which can be calculated by9,40,41 (ΔAσ+ - ΔAσ-)/(ΔAσ+ + ΔAσ-) × 100%. In CHS-Ⅰ, the degree of CTA polarization increases to -40% within 0–20 ps, corresponding to the spin-selective transfer from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3 for generating spin polarization in PbI2. Subsequently, within 20–100 ps, the degree of CTA polarization gradually decays to 0% due to the spin relaxation. We also measured CHS-I samples with 2% and 20% PbI2 (Figure S18), the degree of CTA polarization is below than that of the CHS-I sample with 6% PbI2. At low loading (2%), the chiral R-PbI2/R-NEAPbI3 interfacial area is too small for efficient spin injection, whereas at high loading (20%), excess PbI2 introduces additional defect states as spin-relaxation channels. An intermediate loading of 6% maximizes the effective interfacial area while limiting defect-assisted depolarization, yielding the highest CTA polarization. These demonstrate an inherently long exciton spin relaxation time in CHS-I without circularly polarized light excitation. In contrast, the CTA polarization stabilizes near 0% in CHS-II, indicating that there is no significant spin-selective transfer from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3 in the CHS-II sample. This comparison indicates that the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 and R-PbI2/PbI2 interfaces in CHS-I effectively promote the spin-polarized electron injection from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3, resulting in an increased and sustained degree of CTA polarization of -40%. For comparison, the degree of CTA polarization of pristine R-NEAPbI3 achieves 5% in Figure S19 due to the chirality-induced spin splitting9.

Spin-injection efficiency of a spin-photovoltaic device based on the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure
To quantify the spin-injection efficiency at the interface, a spin-photovoltaic device is fabricated and shown in Figure S20. A key practical parameter of a spin-photovoltaic device is its sensitivity to circularly polarized light, which can be quantified by the degree of photocurrent polarization (DOPcurrent),

DOPcurrent = (Iσ+ - Iσ-)/(Iσ+ + Iσ-) × 100% (4)

where Iσ+ and Iσ- are photocurrents under σ+ and σ- excitations. As shown in Fig. 4a, DOPcurrent is determined by four steps. In the first step, the circularly polarized light excitation at 505 nm selectively excites the PbI2. The σ+ or σ- selectively generates ms=+1/2 or ms=−1/2 electrons and corresponding holes according to the spin-dependent optical selection rule42. The initial degree of spin polarization (P0) generated42 by σ+ or σ- excitation in PbI2 is nearly 100%. Spin depolarization in the second step is due to spin relaxation mechanisms inherent to PbI2, as accounted for by a renormalization factor. The subsequent loss in spin polarization during the third step is determined by the interfacial spin-injection efficiency (Pinj), defined as the differential spin polarization before and after spin injection. Finally, the fourth step’s reduction in spin polarization depends on the spin filtering efficiency (Pfilter) of R-NEAPbI3 due to the CISS effect.

The I–V responses at room temperature for spin-photovoltaic devices based on CHS-I and CHS-II are shown in Fig. 4b,c. The CHS-I device shows distinctly different photocurrent (Iσ+ and Iσ-) in Fig. 4b between σ+ and σ- excitations, despite identical intensities of 1 mW/cm2. Iσ+ is higher than Iσ- because the CISS effect in R-NEAPbI3 selectively favors the transport of electrons with ms=+1/2. In contrast, the CHS-II device exhibits a negligible difference in photocurrent between σ+ and σ- excitations in Fig. 4c. These observations indicate that the difference in photocurrent response under circularly polarized light is due to differences in the loss of spin polarization within the heterostructure. The CHS-I device shows a DOPcurrent of 29%, which is twice as high as that of CHS-II and previously reported chiral MHS heterostructures15,16. To exclude the possibility of sample-to-sample variations, we conducted a statistical analysis of DOPcurrent for CHS-I and CHS-II. The DOPcurrent of CHS-I is 27.9±1.1%, which is higher than the DOPcurrent of CHS-II (9.4±1.8%) (Figure S21). The DOPcurrent of CHS-I device is also higher than the device with only R-NEAPbI3 as the absorber layer (DOPcurrent = 10% as shown in Figure S22). Finally, interfacial spin-injection efficiency can be calculated by12:

Pinj = DOPcurrent / (P0 F Pfilter) (5)

To calculate the Pinj of the device, we assumed a Pfilter of approximately 80% for R-NEAPbI3. This value is derived from established literature on structurally analogous chiral metal-halide systems (containing R-NEA or R-MBA) that share the same spin-filtering geometry, specifically transport along the chiral axis7,8,13,43–45. Figure 4d reveals that Pinj for CHS-Ⅰ increases from 54% at 0.2 V to 68% at −0.4 V. In contrast, Pinj for CHS-Ⅱ remains relatively constant at about 26% over the voltage range studied. The high spin-injection efficiency in CHS-I is attributed to the engineered optimal chiral interface, which leads to the suppression of the interfacial spin scattering46. We therefore conclude that the spin-photovoltaic device based on the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure shows high interfacial spin-injection efficiency, leading to improved CTA and photocurrent polarization, which is correlated with the presence of a helical R-PbI2 layer at the interface. The R-PbI2 layer provides a structurally and chirally matched interface that is associated with efficient spin injection governed by the R-NEAPbI3 layer. Although the spin-injection efficiency of CHS-I reaches up to 68%, DOPcurrent is limited to 29%, primarily due to the renormalization factor (F) of approximately 50%, indicating that nearly half of the spin polarization is lost during spin transport in the PbI2 phase. To further increase F, strategies such as promoting exciton dissociation and extending the spin relaxation time in the PbI2 phase can be considered. Enhancing exciton dissociation may be achieved by decreasing the thickness of the PbI2 layer while maintaining the thickness of the R-PbI2 layer. Additionally, prolonging the spin relaxation time, which is dominated by the Elliott-Yafet mechanism, could be accomplished by operating the device at lower temperatures.

We performed multi-wavelength excitation measurements (405, 450, 488, and 505 nm) on spin-photovoltaic devices based on both CHS-I and CHS-II (details in Figure S23 and Figure S24). For the CHS-I, DOPcurrent is minimized (>10%) when the excitation wavelength approaches the R-NEAPbI3 exciton absorption peak (375 nm) but is maximized (29%) when the PbI2 phase is selectively excited at 505 nm. To extend the spectral response of the spin-photovoltaic devices, bandgap engineering strategies such as halogen doping should be investigated47,48. In contrast, DOPcurrent of the CHS-II device shows minimal variation (±3%) across excitation wavelengths due to its inherently low spin-injection efficiency. Rather than the orientation-sensitive pure R-NEAPbI3 device, where DOPcurrent varies widely (5%–90%) across literature reports24,49–52, our CHS-I device utilizes a chirality-induced grown interface from the same precursor stack without additional process steps. This approach delivers reproducible circularly polarized light detection (29% DOPcurrent) and offers broad applicability to other chiral MHSs.

In this work, we present a synthesis method of interfacial chirality-induced growth that achieves a record-high spin-injection efficiency of 68% in MHSs. Using CTA spectroscopy, we reveal that lattice mismatch, residual strain, and defect density at the interface play a critical role in chiroptical properties. This precisely engineered interface in CHS-I results in a CTA polarization of -40% under linearly polarized light. The spin-photovoltaic device exhibits a maximum photocurrent polarization of 29% at 505 nm, doubling the performance of previous devices. Our findings highlight the important role of the chiral interface for high-performance opto-spintronic applications.
paper_content.methods:
Material preparation
All reagents and materials were purchased from Meyer and Aladdin without further purification. Purchased reagents included (R)-(+)-1-(1-naphthyl)ethylamine (≥98%), hydroiodic acid (47 wt% solution in water, stabilized with ≤ 1.5% hypophosphorous acid), hypophosphorous acid (50 wt% solution in water), and lead iodide (99.99%).

Synthesis of chiral organic ammonium salts
12 mL of organic amine R-NEA was dissolved in 50 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and the vacuum environment was maintained by evacuating and continuously passing nitrogen gas. 20 mL of hydroiodic acid and 2 mL of hypophosphorous acid were slowly injected, and the reaction was stirred continuously at 0 °C for 2 h. The solution was dried under a vacuum at 80 °C for a dash-yellow solid product, which was dissolved in 25 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and 150 mL of anhydrous ether was added to precipitate the product, and the product obtained by filtration was repeated three times to obtain a pure white powder product, i.e., iodine salt of organic amine R-NEAI.

CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ films fabrication
First, a 1.25×1.25 cm2 soda-lime glass was soaked in detergent, purified water, acetone, and isopropanol for ultrasonic cleaning for 15 min, and ultraviolet-ozone treatment for 30 min. Homogeneous R-NEAPbI3 film was synthesized by dissolving 0.9 M PbI2 and 0.9 M R-NEAI in DMF and heating the precursor solution at 70 °C for 1 h. The precursor solution was dropwise added to the treated glass substrate, 10 s at 1000 rpm and 60 s at 5000 rpm during the spin coating process, while 200 μL of chlorobenzene was evenly dropwise added as an anti-solvent at 30 s. The R-NEAPbI3 film was obtained by annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. For the synthesis of CHS-Ⅰ film, the R-NEAPbI3 film was further post-annealed for 15 min, 30 min, 60 min, and 90 min at an ambient atmosphere for inducing the in-growth of PbI2 nanosheets. For the synthesis of CHS-Ⅱ film, 1.2 M PbI2 and 0.9 M R-NEAI in DMF as precursor solution was used, but without post-annealing treatment.

Device fabrication
A circularly polarized photodetector was fabricated in the device configuration of ITO/SnO2 (ETL)/CHS-Ⅰ or CHS-Ⅱ/PbI2 heterostructure/BCP (HTL)/Ag. A 1.5×1.5 cm2 ITO glass was cleaned sequentially with detergent, purified water, acetone, and isopropanol under ultrasonication for 30 min and dried by blowing N2 gas, followed by ultraviolet-ozone treatment for 30 min before spin-coating. The SnO2 colloidal dispersion, diluted with deionized water to be 2 wt%, was spin-coated onto ITO glass at 3000 rpm for 30 s and annealed at 150 °C for 30 min. The R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 heterostructure film was deposited under an ambient atmosphere as described in the film fabrication section. On top of the CHS-Ⅰ or CHS-Ⅱ film, BCP was deposited by thermal evaporation under a vacuum at a pressure of below 8×10-5 Pa. Then, a Ag layer was deposited on the top as a counter electrode by vacuum evaporation. The active area of the device was 2×2 mm2.

General measurements
XRD was performed using a Rigaku Smartlab with Cu Kα radiation source (0.144 nm) and 9 kW power. CD and absorption spectra were measured using the Chirascan circular dichroism spectrometer from Applied Photophysics Ltd. SEM images were obtained using a JXA-8530F Plus field emission electron probe from JEOL Co. Ltd. AFM image was obtained using a Dimension ICON from Bruker. HR-TEM was performed using a JEOL JEM-2100. The current-voltage (I-V) characteristics were recorded by a digital sourcemeter (Keithley 2450). The light sources of 405 nm (GH0406AA2G, SHARP, Japan) and 505 nm (GH05035A2G, SHARP, Japan) were emitted by laser diodes. Unpolarized light was converted to CPL using a quarter-wave plate (Thorlabs) and a linear polarizer (Thorlabs). The light intensity was measured and calibrated by a Si photodetector. Device performance was demonstrated to be stable over a continuous two-days testing period. Furthermore, thin film samples exposed to ambient air for two weeks exhibited negligible variation in their CD signals.

TA and CTA spectroscopy
Transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy was carried out by using a Helios pump-probe system (Ultrafast Systems) combined with a regenerative-amplified Ti: sapphire laser system (Legend Elite-1K-HE, 800 nm, 25 fs, 4 mJ/pulse, and 1 kHz repetition rate) and an optical parametric amplifier system. The output light of a regenerative-amplified Ti: sapphire laser (800 nm) is split into two beams. The main part of the fundamental beam (800 nm) was sent to the optical parametric amplifiers (TOPAS-C), which generated a pump pulse with a tunable wavelength from 290 nm to 2.6 µm. A small part of the fundamental beam (800 nm) was introduced into the TA spectrometer to generate the probe light. After passing through a motorized optical delay line, the 800-nm light beam was attenuated with a neutral density filter and focused on a CaF2 crystal, which was used to generate the white-light continuum (WLC) probe pulses with a wavelength of from 360 to 780 nm, respectively. The probe beam and the pump beam were focused and overlapped onto the sample. The optical path difference between the pump light and the probe light, which was controlled by the motorized optical delay line, was used to get the relative time delay between the probe light and the pump light. After sampling, the probe beam was collimated and then focused into a fiber-coupled spectrometer and detected at a frequency of 1 kHz. Chopped by a synchronized chopper at the frequency of 500 Hz, the pump pulse with a wavelength of 365 nm was modulated such that the TA spectra with and without the pump pulses could be recorded alternately. The intensity of the pump pulse used in the experiment was controlled by a variable neutral-density filter wheel. For the CTA measurement, the circularly polarized pump pulse and the probe pulse were used in the TA measurement. Before the linearly polarized pump pulse and the linearly polarized probe pulse were overlapped onto the sample, they each passed through a double Glan-Taylor calcite polarizer (350–2300 nm, Thorlabs) and a mounted achromatic quarter-wave plate (350–850 nm, Thorlabs). The fast axis of the quarter wave plate was set at 45 or ‒45 degrees to the polarization of the linear pump beam and the linear probe beam to generate a left or right circularly polarized excitation. The circular polarization characteristics were confirmed by polarimeters (Thorlabs). All experiments were performed at room temperature. The analysis was carried out by using Surface Xplorer software.

Computational details
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)53. Projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials were employed54, along with Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functionals55. To match the lattice parameters of R-NEAPbI3, a 3×2 unit cell of PbI2 was used to construct the heterostructure with the R-NEAPbI3 unit cell. The R-NEA-terminated surface of R-NEAPbI3 was in contact with the PbI2 monolayer. To account for van der Waals interactions, we used the dispersion-corrected DFT method56 of Grimme’s D3. The plane-wave cutoff energy was set to 520 eV, and the first Brillouin zone was sampled using a 3×3×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid for the structure optimization of the heterostructure. The ionic positions were fully relaxed until the total energies and forces were less than 10-6 eV and 0.02 eV/Å, respectively.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This work presents a study of how an interlayer of R-PbI2 play an important role in spin-photovoltaic device to improve spin injection efficiency. While the concept is novel and the device results demonstrate some functional merit, several claims lack solid experimental substantiation. Certain findings do not conclusively support the authors' proposed conclusions. Additionally, the logical flow of the manuscript is disjointed. I recommend major revision addressing all concerns below before reconsideration for publication.
Here's my questions and comments:
1. The author proposed that the XRD peak increases indicates grain size decrease due to partially converted to R-PbI2. But this only happens at the interface between R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2, I don’t think it can result in a notable XRD peak change.
2. The author mentions there should be no byproduct (R-NEA)2PbI4. However, in Figure 1c, the shoulder around 400nm looks like (R-NEA)2PbI4 exciton absorption.
3. The CD in Figure 1d only gives R enantiomer’s data, we know that there could be artifact such as LDLB resulting in CD signal. I’d like to see CD responses of S enantiomer and racemic sample.
4. The AFM in Figure 1e shows that the PbI2 are flakes inserted vertically in R-NEAPbI3. What is the direction of the chiral axis of R-PbI2? Does it allow CISS to filter spin carriers transported across the interface?
5. The authors discussed two kinds of heterostructures, one with R-PbI2, one without R-PbI2. For the CHS-II, there is no post-annealing process. How do you know it is a heterostructure of R-NEAPbI3 layer and PbI2 layer rather than a mixture of NEAPbI3 and PbI2. In my opinion you can not rule out this possibility.
6. The authors states:” The R-PbI2 in CHS-I reduces the interfacial lattice mismatch to 5.4%, compared to an 8.4% mismatch observed in CHS-Ⅱ.” What’s the evidence of this statement?
7. From I-V characteristics, the authors conclude that R-PbI2 passivates interfacial defect states. Can you explain the mechanism of this passivation?
8. In Figure 2f, CHS-II gives a shorter lifetime than CHS-I, does that mean more efficient exciton dissociation than CHS-I?
9. In Figure 3, the authors discussed spin dynamics of the heterostructure. However, I don’t think the lifetime measured by CP-TA is spin relaxation time people talked about in the field of spintronics. Therefore, discussion about the EY mechanism is not appropriate. Moreover, EY mechanism refers to spin relaxation by phonon scattering caused by SOC, which should not be related to bandgap. And it’s hard to believe a bandgap different of ~0.1 eV shown in Figure S10 can be resulted from a few nm of R-PbI2.
10. As the authors calculated the renormalization factors F for CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ to be 53.2±2.5% and 52.6±4.2%. From an experimental science perspective, it cannot be concluded that F for CHS-I is statistically greater than for CHS-II.
11. In the spin photovoltaic device study shown in Figure 4, 505nm excitation light is used, which only excites PbI2. Therefore, in the devices only PbI2 is the active layer and R-NEAPbI3 only serves as a charge transport layer. CHS-I shows better performance than CHS-II due to the existence of R-PbI2. But this is not the case in most photovoltaic devices. A more rational approach would be using light that can also excite R-NEAPbI3, followed by comparative analysis of the performance of CHS-I and CHS-II.
12. Is this method of forming R-PbI2 at interface can be used in other chiral perovskite system? Because R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 are not good choice for photovoltaic application. And the FF and efficiency shown in Figure 4 is quite small. If this R-PbI2 can only be synthesized in this material, I don’t think it is significant enough for the field of spintronics and optoelectronics.

The manuscript by Jin Xiao and co-workers reports the atomic-precision synthesis of chiral interfaces by developing an interfacial chirality-induced growth approach. The authors demonstrate that the few-nanometre-thick chiral lead iodide (R-PbI2) reduced lattice mismatch, residual strain, and defect density at interfaces. More importantly, the precisely engineered chiral interfaces contribute to the interfacial spin injection, which is one of the key challenges for realizing opto-spintronic applications. This manuscript is logically clear and inspiring to the research community. Therefore, I recommend that this paper be accepted by Nature Communications after some minor revisions.
1. Although the obvious circular dichroism signal at the exciton absorption peak of PbI2 is one of the important pieces of evidence of chiral interfaces. However, the circular dichroism signal may stem from macroscopic anisotropy of thin films. How to determine whether this circular dichroism signal is due to the intrinsic chirality of R-PbI2 rather than the macroscopic anisotropy of thin films?
2. In the device demonstration, the spin-injection efficiency is as high as 68%, so why is the photocurrent polarization only 40%? What methods are there to improve the photocurrent polarization in the future?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is a review of “Atomic-precision synthesis of chiral interface in the heterostructure for efficient spin injection” by Xiao et. al. In this study the authors measured the circular polarized light detection efficiency of a photo-diode composed of a hybrid metal halide semiconductor coupled to a light absorption PbI2 layer. Their main claim is that by modifying the interface between the PbI2 and MHS to be a helical interface they are able to increase drastically the efficiency of the CPL, indicating that interface effects are very important.
The first part of the paper describes the synthesis and characterization of the fabricated layers, and the second part compares between a bilayer without the helical interface and a bilayer with the interface.
The premise of the study is of interest to the community and the results could be interesting. But there are a lot of questions that need addressing to ensure the results presented are correct and not only circumstantial.
Below I list these concerns and will highlight the most important in my opinion. I am not an expert in the MHS synthesis, so I cannot assess this part of the manuscript, and leave the review of this part to other referees.
Main issue. In ref. 23 of this paper the authors study the same (R/S-NEA)PbI3 hybrid perovskite and use this layer as the CPL absorber layer. In this paper the authros claim that only the PI2 is the CPL absorbing layer, which requires the important interface. It seems to me that from a practical application perspective they have only complicated the device. From basic physics it is still interesting. But since they put an emphasis on the applicability of the research – they must address the criticism or reframe their study in another way.
It is not clear what is the spread and reproducibility of the study results. It is necessary to show in the supplementary an additional device of each kind to see the differences in order to support the claims regarding the percentages stated in this paper.

I ask the authors to disproof this by adding results of at least pump probe of another sample. I mean, if you prepare a sample then you do the pump probe. You do not choose just one sample for this experiment. This is not good science.
Small comment regarding defect analysis line 144. I don’t know if the defect changes may be from sample-to-sample variations or they are really from some passivation effects. Such changes are seen in different samples. Please comment what was your difference between samples.
Line 181-184 the authors discuss the renormalization factor F . Values from both samples are identical in the uncertainty of the measurement. It is incorrect to claim that was is larger than the other, and that it indicates the interface facilitates spin transport, which is the main claim of this paper.
In three different parts of the article the authors use 3 different wavelengths. The choice is unclear. If it is due to instrument limitations just say so. But for the spin injection experiment a wavelength dependent effect is very important. It would be great if the authors could show results not only for 505nm.
Small comment - DOP in line 212 was not explicitly defined. Also – why not plot DOP and not just claim a value.
In line 224 the comparison of the citation is to different systems, so they have to justify why they can assume that P_filter is the same in their sample.

It indicates there is an error in their experiment, e.g. the background was not calculated correctly, adding an offset for Delta_A, since the data does look just shifted and not relaxing. Small comment in the next line 201 the authors state “CHS-II exhibits similar initial spin dynamics”. I don’t see any similarity in the initial spin dynamics.

The crystal relieves this strain by forming structural imperfections, principally grain boundaries and dislocations. In the case of CHS-I, the formation of the R-PbI phase at the interface improves the structural transition between layers. This technique uses a circularly polarized pump pulse to preferentially generate a spin-polarized population of excitons. The subsequent evolution of this spin polarization is monitored by a probe pulse that selectively measures the populations of distinct total angular momentum states J 7 ±1). Because each J state is composed of a unique combination of electron and hole spins, monitoring their population changes over time allows us to directly observe spin relaxation processes. The resulting pump-probe signal, which is proportional to the exciton population, is then fitted with a kinetic model to quantify the spin relaxation time (T ), as described previously [Nano Lett., 2015, 15, 1553–1558; Nat Commun, 2020, 11, 5665; Adv. The hyperfine interaction is generally significant only in systems with weak spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and abundant nuclear spins, such as organic semiconductors, rather than metal halide semiconductors. ## Abstract

Precise control of interfaces is crucial for spin generation, transport, and detection in opto-spintronics. However, the interface engineering for efficient spin injection remains a significant challenge. Here, we synthesized a helical structure of PbI2 (R-PbI2) via an interfacial chirality-induced growth approach at the heterostructure interface. This few-nanometer-thick R-PbI2 layer shows a lower lattice mismatch with both the adjacent R-NEAPbI3 (R-NEA refers to R-1-(1-naphtyl)ethylamine) and PbI2 layers, and leads to an optimal chiral interface in the chiral heterostructure with minimized residual strain and defect density. Combined with circularly polarized pump-probe spectroscopic and spin-photovoltaic measurements, our chiral heterostructure interface contributes a spin-injection efficiency up to 68%, thus leading to a degree of polarization of 29% in photocurrent. The precise synthesis of a chiral interface offers a promising route to manipulate spin dynamics and achieve a high degree of spin polarization required for advanced opto-spintronic applications.

---

## Introduction

The generation of spin-polarized charge carriers in semiconductors is the fundamental prerequisite for opto-spintronics1–3. Major approaches for generating spin-polarized carriers rely on spin injection by ferromagnetic contact or circularly polarized light4,5, but typically require cryogenic temperatures, external magnetic fields, or precise optical alignment. Recently, chiral metal halide semiconductors (MHSs) have emerged as promising materials in opto-spintronics due to their strong spin-orbit coupling and chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS)6–9, enabling room-temperature spin polarization without external magnetic fields. However, insulating chiral organic components lead to relatively poor charge transport and electron-phonon spin depolarization, which limits their performance10,11. Heterostructures that consist of chiral MHSs and achiral semiconductors have been demonstrated to enhance the charge transport and the degree of polarization12–16. This approach synergistically combines the spin selectivity of chiral MHSs with the optoelectronic properties of achiral semiconductors17–19.

The interface plays a critical role in both optoelectronic and spintronic applications. In optoelectronics, its precise characteristics control charge separation and recombination, directly impacting performance. For spintronics, the interface is crucial for the effective injection, manipulation, and detection of spin-polarized carriers. Therefore, the selection of a robust fabrication method for the heterostructure is essential. Previous heterostructure fabrication methods include dry-transfer stacking18, hot-casting14, solution-based spin-coating20, and self-assembly21. The interfacial characteristics in terms of morphology, defect density, bonding, and chemical interaction in chiral MHS heterostructures can govern their functional properties, particularly charge transfer, spin dynamics, and chiroptical responses. Dry-transfer method generally aims for chemically inert interfaces to preserve the integrity of the constituent layers18. Hot-casting method relies on specific and designed chemical bonds14. Spin-coating and self-assembly methods can involve interfacial chemical transformations, which might be leveraged for in-situ tuning of properties but also pose challenges in predictability20,21.

Here, we synthesize chiral MHS heterostructures by an interfacial chirality-induced growth approach with PbI2 and R-NEAI (R-NEA denotes R-1-(1-naphtyl)ethylamine) solutions. The chiral interface is engineered with a high-crystallinity and helical R-PbI2 layer, which effectively suppresses interfacial spin depolarization and leads to a spin-injection efficiency of up to 68%. Our results demonstrate that lattice mismatch, residual strain, and defect density at the interface are critical factors for spin-injection efficiency. A spin-photovoltaic device of R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure achieves 29% degree of polarization in photocurrent, twice that of previously reported chiral MHS heterostructures15,16. This chiral MHS heterostructure growth approach paves the way for efficient spin injection and a high degree of spin polarization at room temperature, advancing the development of opto-spintronic applications.

---

## Results

Synthesis of the chiral interface by an interfacial chirality-induced growth method
We spin-coated a precursor solution containing equimolar amounts of PbI2 and R-NEAI onto a glass substrate, followed by annealing at 100 °C for 5 min to grow the R-NEAPbI3 film. Subsequently, the film was post-annealed at 100 °C in air to in-situ grow the PbI2 layer on the top of R-NEAPbI3 (details are provided in the Method). The delocalized R-NEA+ cations between R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 induced a chiral lattice deformation of PbI2 by interfacial chirality transfer22, shown in Fig. 1a. In the post-annealing process, the R-NEAPbI3 is mainly converted into PbI2, with only a small amount of conversion to a few-nanometer-thickness R-PbI2 between R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2. The R-NEAPbI3 phase content decreased with increasing annealing time, while the PbI2 content correspondingly increased. From the in-situ X-ray diffraction spectra in Fig. 1b, the peak at 12.7° refers to the (001) peak of the PbI2 phase and becomes prominent with increasing annealing time. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the (002) peak of the R-NEAPbI3 phase slightly increases from 0.16° to 0.18° with the annealing time. The increase in FWHM of the (002) peak of R-NEAPbI3 is mainly due to the precipitation of PbI2, which reduces the grain size of the remaining R-NEAPbI3 domains, as estimated from the Scherrer equation23. The in-situ X-ray diffraction spectra show that there is no by-product (R-NEA)2PbI4, whose diffraction peak of the (002) plane is at 5.8° (Figure S1). The PbI2 content can be estimated by the energy-dispersive X-ray spectra shown in Figure S2. We achieved 6% PbI2 after 30 min of post-annealing.

In Fig. 1c, as the post-annealing time increases, R-NEAPbI3 is partially converted into PbI2, evidenced by the weakening of the R-NEAPbI3 absorption peak24 at 375 nm and the strengthening of the PbI2 absorption peak25 at 500 nm (detailed analysis in Figure S3). In Fig. 1d, a pair of reverse circular dichroism (CD) peaks at 376 nm and 408 nm corresponds to the excitonic absorption of R-NEAPbI3. Additionally, shoulders near 500 nm in CD spectra are caused by the excitonic absorption of PbI2 rather than (R-NEA)2PbI4. These shoulders become more pronounced with increasing PbI2 content, suggesting that the PbI2 lattice undergoes chiral deformation. The absorption dissymmetry factor, gCD, at 500 nm reaches a maximum value of 0.02 at a PbI2 concentration of 6% (Figure S4). Consequently, CHS-I at this concentration was selected for subsequent research, as it yielded R-PbI2 with the highest relative proportion of PbI2.

A comparable CD spectral feature appears in the S-configuration samples, though with reversed polarity (Figure S5). In contrast, the racemic sample exhibits no CD response (Figure S5). To distinguish the true CD signal from artifacts arising from linear circular dichroism and linear birefringence, we extracted the genuine CD signal following established methods26 (detailed analysis in Supplementary Information). This genuine signal persists at 500 nm corresponds to the exciton absorption peak of PbI2, indicating that the shoulder peak at this wavelength originates from the intrinsic chirality of R-PbI2 rather than experimental artifacts. To assess the universality of this interfacial chirality-induced growth method, we performed post-annealing treatments on 1D R-MBAPbI3, 2D (R-MBA)2PbI4, and 2D (R-4-Br-MBA)2PbI4 (where R-MBA and R-4-Br-MBA denote R-1-phenylethanamine and R-1-(4-bromophenyl)ethanamine, respectively). In these films, the CD signal near 500 nm increases significantly with extended post-annealing time, a trend attributed to the formation of R-PbI2 (Figure S6).

This lattice distortion is further supported by our DFT calculations (details in Supplementary Information and Figure S7). The deformation is attributed to asymmetric hydrogen bonding (H2N–H···I) between the iodine atoms of PbI2 and R-NEA+ at the interface, which induces structure distortion in PbI2 and leads to the formation of a chiral R-PbI2 layer. The chiral axis of R-PbI2 is parallel to the in-plane direction of R-NEAPbI3. From the atomic force microscopic image in Fig. 1e, PbI2 grown on top of the R-NEAPbI3 shows a flake-like structure and inserted vertically into the R-NEAPbI3 layer. The PbI2 flakes have a length of 1.2±0.3 μm, a width of 39±8 nm, and a thickness of 145±0.5 nm. The size and distribution of PbI2 flakes can be tuned by changing the post-annealing time (see Figure S8 for more details).

We characterized the lattice structure using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) in Fig. 1f. The image reveals two distinct lattice structures in the heterostructure, a lattice spacing of 0.362 nm, corresponding to the (013) plane of R-NEAPbI3, and a lattice spacing of 0.338 nm and 0.348 nm, associated with the (002) plane of PbI2 and R-PbI2, respectively. Using Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms, we isolated the (002) plane of PbI2 at the interface by applying a mask. Within a 5 nm-thick region at the interface, detailed analysis reveals a helical lattice distortion featuring a spiral radius of 0.02 nm and a pitch of 0.84 nm. These observations agree with our DFT calculations. The interface exhibits chirality because the helically arranged R-NEA+ cations transfer their chiral information to the adjacent PbI2, inducing a helical structure in the PbI2.

Chiral heterostructure interface characterizations
Two different chiral MHS heterostructures are synthesized to demonstrate the critical role of the R-PbI2 layer at the interface. CHS-I refers to the heterostructure with R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 and R-PbI2/PbI2 interfaces, and CHS-II refers to the heterostructure with only R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 interface. CHS-II is synthesized without interfacial chirality-induced growth, resulting in PbI2 forming nanoparticles with a diameter of 150±20 nm. The PbI2 nanoparticles is embedded within R-NEAPbI3 layer, as shown in Figure S9. CD response and gCD are zero at 500 nm regardless of the PbI2 content27 (Figure S10), indicating the absence of helical lattice distortion in PbI2 of CHS-II.

In Fig. 2a, we plot the schematic lattice structures of both CHS-I and CHS-II. In CHS-II, the lattice mismatch is mainly located at the R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 interface, whereas in CHS-I, it is primarily at the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 interface. HR-TEM analysis in Fig. 1f reveals that the R-NEAPbI3 (103) plane contacts the PbI2 or R-PbI2 (002) plane, with lattice fringes intersecting at approximately 65°. We calculated the interfacial lattice mismatch28 using the measured interplanar spacings, d(103)=0.362 nm for R-NEAPbI3, d(002)=0.338 nm for PbI2, and d'(002)=0.348 nm for R-PbI2. This yields a lattice mismatch of 3.9% for CHS-I and 6.6% for CHS-II. The lower lattice mismatch in CHS-I shows that the R-PbI2 interlayer effectively relieves the interfacial lattice mismatch. Then we used grazing incident X-ray diffraction spectra shown in Figure S11 and related 2θ vs sin2φ plot in Fig. 2b to characterize the residual strain distribution in CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ. The tensile strain is determined from the slope of 2θ vs sin2φ plot29,30, yielding 0.42% for CHS-I and 1.48% for CHS-II. This reduced tensile strain in CHS-I is attributed to the flexibility of the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 interface31.

The defect densities of CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ were evaluated using the space-charge-limited current method (device configurations are in Figure S12), as shown in Fig. 2c,d. The current (I) initially increases linearly with voltage (V), which is the ohmic response. Then the current rises exponentially (I/Vn, n>2) at 0.14 V for CHS-I and 0.4 V for CHS-II, indicating a transition to the trap-filled limit (TFL), in which all the available trap (defect) states are filled by the injected carriers32. The onset voltage is determined by:

VTFL = en d L2 / 2εrε0 (1)

where L is film thickness, εr is the permittivity, and ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, and nd is the defect density33,34. Notably, nd in CHS-I is 0.39×1016 cm-3, approximately one-third that of CHS-II (1.10×1016 cm-3). To exclude sample-to-sample variability as the cause of the reduced defect density, we fabricated multiple devices for both CHS-I and CHS-II under identical synthesis and processing conditions (Figure S13). The nd of CHS-I is (0.38±0.04)×1016 cm-3, which is lower than that of CHS-II [(1.26±0.59)×1016 cm-3], indicating that CHS-I possesses a more efficient passivation mechanism than CHS-II. For CHS-I, post-annealing partially decomposes R-NEAPbI3 into PbI2 and R-NEAI, enriching the interface with excess R-NEA+ and I-. The R-NEA+ cations act as Lewis bases to passivate undercoordinated Pb and Pb vacancies, while I- compensates iodide vacancies, thereby reducing the interfacial defect density35.

To investigate the exciton dynamics in the heterostructure, we performed transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy using a linearly polarized pump pulse of 365 nm wavelength and a broadband linearly polarized probe. Figure 2e,f show the absorption difference between pump and probe (ΔA = Apump on - Apump off) from TA spectra. Figure 2e exhibits distinct ground state bleaching (GSB) signals at 410 nm and 500 nm for R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2, respectively. There are two photo-induced absorption signals at 450 nm and 520 nm for R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2, respectively. It indicates that excitons are formed after photo-excitation of R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 in the heterostructure. Figure 2f shows the time evolution of excitons probed in the GSB region at 500 nm. The TA signals exhibit mono-exponential decay kinetics, yielding an exciton lifetime of 16.9±0.3 ps for CHS-Ⅰ, which is longer than the 8.3±0.3 ps measured for CHS-Ⅱ. The exciton lifetime in CHS-I or CHS-II is shorter compared to that of pristine PbI2 (26.2±0.9 ps, Figure S14) due to promoted exciton dissociation in the type-II heterojunction formed by R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 heterostructure21. The shorter exciton lifetime in CHS-II (Fig. 2f) indicates more efficient exciton dissociation and charge transfer, consistent with the bulk heterostructure formed by PbI2 nanoparticles distributed throughout the R-NEAPbI3 matrix36. In contrast, the PbI2 nanosheets, vertically inserted R-NEAPbI3 matrix in CHS-I, provide a smaller interfacial area, leading to slower exciton dissociation and a longer lifetime.

Modulation of exciton spin dynamics at the chiral interface
We investigated the exciton spin polarization dynamics in the heterostructures at room temperature using circularly polarized TA (CTA) spectroscopy (schematic in Fig. 3a). A right-circularly polarized (σ+) pump pulse at 365 nm selectively generated excitons with angular momentum J=+1 in both PbI2 phase and R-NEAPbI3 phase. The exciton spin relaxation of this initial +1 state can lead to the formation of -1 exciton via spin-flip37. The subsequent dynamics were monitored by probing the TA spectra with broadband right- or left-circularly polarized light (σ+ or σ-). The time evolution of TA spectra collected at 500 nm with co-circular (σ+σ+) and cross-circular (σ+σ-) pump-probe configurations are shown in Fig. 3b,c. The relaxation of exciton spin polarization is evaluated by the difference between the TA signals obtained with co-circular and cross-circular configurations (ΔAσ+σ- - ΔAσ+σ+). Exponential fitting of the decay curves yields exciton spin relaxation times of 19.2±1.9 ps for the PbI2 phase in CHS-Ⅰ and 9.2±1.5 ps in CHS-Ⅱ, respectively. Based on temperature-dependent and pump fluence-dependent spin relaxation time, we determine that the spin relaxation in PbI2 is dominated by the Elliott-Yafet mechanism (details in Figure S15 and Figure S16). The spin relaxation time and bandgap of PbI2 are positively correlated38,

τE ∝ 1 / (E - Δso)2 E T2 τp (2)

where Δso is the spin-orbit splitting of the valence band, Eg is bandgap, T is temperature, τp is momentum relaxation time. A 0.06 eV bandgap increase in CHS-I (Figure S17) arises mainly from the PbI2 morphology rather than the few-nanometer R-PbI2 layer. The thickness of PbI2 in CHS-I (39±8 nm) is much thinner than that of CHS-II (150±20 nm), leading to stronger quantum confinement and thus a larger bandgap39, which in turn prolongs the exciton spin relaxation time in the PbI2 phase of CHS-I. The exciton lifetime τ and spin relaxation time τs determine the fraction of spin-polarized electrons before the spin injection at the interface, that is, a renormalization factor12:

F = 1 / (1 + τ / τs) (3)

The renormalization factors F for CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ are 53.2±2.5% and 52.6±4.2%, respectively, indicating that the initial spin polarization created by the light within the PbI2 layer is comparable for both samples. In contrast to typical TA spectra, where circularly polarized excitation directly induces spin polarization, the observed spin splitting between σ+ and σ- probe spectra under linearly polarized excitation must arise from the spin-selective electron transfer at the heterojunction (schematic in Fig. 3d). The excitation wavelength of linearly polarized pump pulse is fixed at 465 nm rather than 500 nm to selectively excite PbI2 phase and avoid the interference between the R-NEAPbI3 and PbI2 excitons in the GSB region (500 nm), respectively. We measured the TA spectra with linear pump and σ+ or σ- probe, which are plotted in Fig. 3e,f. The degree of CTA polarization in PbI2 represents the degree of spin polarization between excitons with J=+1 and J=−1, which can be calculated by9,40,41 (ΔAσ+ - ΔAσ-)/(ΔAσ+ + ΔAσ-) × 100%. In CHS-Ⅰ, the degree of CTA polarization increases to -40% within 0–20 ps, corresponding to the spin-selective transfer from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3 for generating spin polarization in PbI2. Subsequently, within 20–100 ps, the degree of CTA polarization gradually decays to 0% due to the spin relaxation. We also measured CHS-I samples with 2% and 20% PbI2 (Figure S18), the degree of CTA polarization is below than that of the CHS-I sample with 6% PbI2. At low loading (2%), the chiral R-PbI2/R-NEAPbI3 interfacial area is too small for efficient spin injection, whereas at high loading (20%), excess PbI2 introduces additional defect states as spin-relaxation channels. An intermediate loading of 6% maximizes the effective interfacial area while limiting defect-assisted depolarization, yielding the highest CTA polarization. These demonstrate an inherently long exciton spin relaxation time in CHS-I without circularly polarized light excitation. In contrast, the CTA polarization stabilizes near 0% in CHS-II, indicating that there is no significant spin-selective transfer from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3 in the CHS-II sample. This comparison indicates that the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2 and R-PbI2/PbI2 interfaces in CHS-I effectively promote the spin-polarized electron injection from PbI2 to R-NEAPbI3, resulting in an increased and sustained degree of CTA polarization of -40%. For comparison, the degree of CTA polarization of pristine R-NEAPbI3 achieves 5% in Figure S19 due to the chirality-induced spin splitting9.

Spin-injection efficiency of a spin-photovoltaic device based on the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure
To quantify the spin-injection efficiency at the interface, a spin-photovoltaic device is fabricated and shown in Figure S20. A key practical parameter of a spin-photovoltaic device is its sensitivity to circularly polarized light, which can be quantified by the degree of photocurrent polarization (DOPcurrent),

DOPcurrent = (Iσ+ - Iσ-)/(Iσ+ + Iσ-) × 100% (4)

where Iσ+ and Iσ- are photocurrents under σ+ and σ- excitations. As shown in Fig. 4a, DOPcurrent is determined by four steps. In the first step, the circularly polarized light excitation at 505 nm selectively excites the PbI2. The σ+ or σ- selectively generates ms=+1/2 or ms=−1/2 electrons and corresponding holes according to the spin-dependent optical selection rule42. The initial degree of spin polarization (P0) generated42 by σ+ or σ- excitation in PbI2 is nearly 100%. Spin depolarization in the second step is due to spin relaxation mechanisms inherent to PbI2, as accounted for by a renormalization factor. The subsequent loss in spin polarization during the third step is determined by the interfacial spin-injection efficiency (Pinj), defined as the differential spin polarization before and after spin injection. Finally, the fourth step’s reduction in spin polarization depends on the spin filtering efficiency (Pfilter) of R-NEAPbI3 due to the CISS effect.

The I–V responses at room temperature for spin-photovoltaic devices based on CHS-I and CHS-II are shown in Fig. 4b,c. The CHS-I device shows distinctly different photocurrent (Iσ+ and Iσ-) in Fig. 4b between σ+ and σ- excitations, despite identical intensities of 1 mW/cm2. Iσ+ is higher than Iσ- because the CISS effect in R-NEAPbI3 selectively favors the transport of electrons with ms=+1/2. In contrast, the CHS-II device exhibits a negligible difference in photocurrent between σ+ and σ- excitations in Fig. 4c. These observations indicate that the difference in photocurrent response under circularly polarized light is due to differences in the loss of spin polarization within the heterostructure. The CHS-I device shows a DOPcurrent of 29%, which is twice as high as that of CHS-II and previously reported chiral MHS heterostructures15,16. To exclude the possibility of sample-to-sample variations, we conducted a statistical analysis of DOPcurrent for CHS-I and CHS-II. The DOPcurrent of CHS-I is 27.9±1.1%, which is higher than the DOPcurrent of CHS-II (9.4±1.8%) (Figure S21). The DOPcurrent of CHS-I device is also higher than the device with only R-NEAPbI3 as the absorber layer (DOPcurrent = 10% as shown in Figure S22). Finally, interfacial spin-injection efficiency can be calculated by12:

Pinj = DOPcurrent / (P0 F Pfilter) (5)

To calculate the Pinj of the device, we assumed a Pfilter of approximately 80% for R-NEAPbI3. This value is derived from established literature on structurally analogous chiral metal-halide systems (containing R-NEA or R-MBA) that share the same spin-filtering geometry, specifically transport along the chiral axis7,8,13,43–45. Figure 4d reveals that Pinj for CHS-Ⅰ increases from 54% at 0.2 V to 68% at −0.4 V. In contrast, Pinj for CHS-Ⅱ remains relatively constant at about 26% over the voltage range studied. The high spin-injection efficiency in CHS-I is attributed to the engineered optimal chiral interface, which leads to the suppression of the interfacial spin scattering46. We therefore conclude that the spin-photovoltaic device based on the R-NEAPbI3/R-PbI2/PbI2 heterostructure shows high interfacial spin-injection efficiency, leading to improved CTA and photocurrent polarization, which is correlated with the presence of a helical R-PbI2 layer at the interface. The R-PbI2 layer provides a structurally and chirally matched interface that is associated with efficient spin injection governed by the R-NEAPbI3 layer. Although the spin-injection efficiency of CHS-I reaches up to 68%, DOPcurrent is limited to 29%, primarily due to the renormalization factor (F) of approximately 50%, indicating that nearly half of the spin polarization is lost during spin transport in the PbI2 phase. To further increase F, strategies such as promoting exciton dissociation and extending the spin relaxation time in the PbI2 phase can be considered. Enhancing exciton dissociation may be achieved by decreasing the thickness of the PbI2 layer while maintaining the thickness of the R-PbI2 layer. Additionally, prolonging the spin relaxation time, which is dominated by the Elliott-Yafet mechanism, could be accomplished by operating the device at lower temperatures.

We performed multi-wavelength excitation measurements (405, 450, 488, and 505 nm) on spin-photovoltaic devices based on both CHS-I and CHS-II (details in Figure S23 and Figure S24). For the CHS-I, DOPcurrent is minimized (>10%) when the excitation wavelength approaches the R-NEAPbI3 exciton absorption peak (375 nm) but is maximized (29%) when the PbI2 phase is selectively excited at 505 nm. To extend the spectral response of the spin-photovoltaic devices, bandgap engineering strategies such as halogen doping should be investigated47,48. In contrast, DOPcurrent of the CHS-II device shows minimal variation (±3%) across excitation wavelengths due to its inherently low spin-injection efficiency. Rather than the orientation-sensitive pure R-NEAPbI3 device, where DOPcurrent varies widely (5%–90%) across literature reports24,49–52, our CHS-I device utilizes a chirality-induced grown interface from the same precursor stack without additional process steps. This approach delivers reproducible circularly polarized light detection (29% DOPcurrent) and offers broad applicability to other chiral MHSs.

In this work, we present a synthesis method of interfacial chirality-induced growth that achieves a record-high spin-injection efficiency of 68% in MHSs. Using CTA spectroscopy, we reveal that lattice mismatch, residual strain, and defect density at the interface play a critical role in chiroptical properties. This precisely engineered interface in CHS-I results in a CTA polarization of -40% under linearly polarized light. The spin-photovoltaic device exhibits a maximum photocurrent polarization of 29% at 505 nm, doubling the performance of previous devices. Our findings highlight the important role of the chiral interface for high-performance opto-spintronic applications.

---

## Methods

Material preparation
All reagents and materials were purchased from Meyer and Aladdin without further purification. Purchased reagents included (R)-(+)-1-(1-naphthyl)ethylamine (≥98%), hydroiodic acid (47 wt% solution in water, stabilized with ≤ 1.5% hypophosphorous acid), hypophosphorous acid (50 wt% solution in water), and lead iodide (99.99%).

Synthesis of chiral organic ammonium salts
12 mL of organic amine R-NEA was dissolved in 50 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and the vacuum environment was maintained by evacuating and continuously passing nitrogen gas. 20 mL of hydroiodic acid and 2 mL of hypophosphorous acid were slowly injected, and the reaction was stirred continuously at 0 °C for 2 h. The solution was dried under a vacuum at 80 °C for a dash-yellow solid product, which was dissolved in 25 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and 150 mL of anhydrous ether was added to precipitate the product, and the product obtained by filtration was repeated three times to obtain a pure white powder product, i.e., iodine salt of organic amine R-NEAI.

CHS-Ⅰ and CHS-Ⅱ films fabrication
First, a 1.25×1.25 cm2 soda-lime glass was soaked in detergent, purified water, acetone, and isopropanol for ultrasonic cleaning for 15 min, and ultraviolet-ozone treatment for 30 min. Homogeneous R-NEAPbI3 film was synthesized by dissolving 0.9 M PbI2 and 0.9 M R-NEAI in DMF and heating the precursor solution at 70 °C for 1 h. The precursor solution was dropwise added to the treated glass substrate, 10 s at 1000 rpm and 60 s at 5000 rpm during the spin coating process, while 200 μL of chlorobenzene was evenly dropwise added as an anti-solvent at 30 s. The R-NEAPbI3 film was obtained by annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. For the synthesis of CHS-Ⅰ film, the R-NEAPbI3 film was further post-annealed for 15 min, 30 min, 60 min, and 90 min at an ambient atmosphere for inducing the in-growth of PbI2 nanosheets. For the synthesis of CHS-Ⅱ film, 1.2 M PbI2 and 0.9 M R-NEAI in DMF as precursor solution was used, but without post-annealing treatment.

Device fabrication
A circularly polarized photodetector was fabricated in the device configuration of ITO/SnO2 (ETL)/CHS-Ⅰ or CHS-Ⅱ/PbI2 heterostructure/BCP (HTL)/Ag. A 1.5×1.5 cm2 ITO glass was cleaned sequentially with detergent, purified water, acetone, and isopropanol under ultrasonication for 30 min and dried by blowing N2 gas, followed by ultraviolet-ozone treatment for 30 min before spin-coating. The SnO2 colloidal dispersion, diluted with deionized water to be 2 wt%, was spin-coated onto ITO glass at 3000 rpm for 30 s and annealed at 150 °C for 30 min. The R-NEAPbI3/PbI2 heterostructure film was deposited under an ambient atmosphere as described in the film fabrication section. On top of the CHS-Ⅰ or CHS-Ⅱ film, BCP was deposited by thermal evaporation under a vacuum at a pressure of below 8×10-5 Pa. Then, a Ag layer was deposited on the top as a counter electrode by vacuum evaporation. The active area of the device was 2×2 mm2.

General measurements
XRD was performed using a Rigaku Smartlab with Cu Kα radiation source (0.144 nm) and 9 kW power. CD and absorption spectra were measured using the Chirascan circular dichroism spectrometer from Applied Photophysics Ltd. SEM images were obtained using a JXA-8530F Plus field emission electron probe from JEOL Co. Ltd. AFM image was obtained using a Dimension ICON from Bruker. HR-TEM was performed using a JEOL JEM-2100. The current-voltage (I-V) characteristics were recorded by a digital sourcemeter (Keithley 2450). The light sources of 405 nm (GH0406AA2G, SHARP, Japan) and 505 nm (GH05035A2G, SHARP, Japan) were emitted by laser diodes. Unpolarized light was converted to CPL using a quarter-wave plate (Thorlabs) and a linear polarizer (Thorlabs). The light intensity was measured and calibrated by a Si photodetector. Device performance was demonstrated to be stable over a continuous two-days testing period. Furthermore, thin film samples exposed to ambient air for two weeks exhibited negligible variation in their CD signals.

TA and CTA spectroscopy
Transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy was carried out by using a Helios pump-probe system (Ultrafast Systems) combined with a regenerative-amplified Ti: sapphire laser system (Legend Elite-1K-HE, 800 nm, 25 fs, 4 mJ/pulse, and 1 kHz repetition rate) and an optical parametric amplifier system. The output light of a regenerative-amplified Ti: sapphire laser (800 nm) is split into two beams. The main part of the fundamental beam (800 nm) was sent to the optical parametric amplifiers (TOPAS-C), which generated a pump pulse with a tunable wavelength from 290 nm to 2.6 µm. A small part of the fundamental beam (800 nm) was introduced into the TA spectrometer to generate the probe light. After passing through a motorized optical delay line, the 800-nm light beam was attenuated with a neutral density filter and focused on a CaF2 crystal, which was used to generate the white-light continuum (WLC) probe pulses with a wavelength of from 360 to 780 nm, respectively. The probe beam and the pump beam were focused and overlapped onto the sample. The optical path difference between the pump light and the probe light, which was controlled by the motorized optical delay line, was used to get the relative time delay between the probe light and the pump light. After sampling, the probe beam was collimated and then focused into a fiber-coupled spectrometer and detected at a frequency of 1 kHz. Chopped by a synchronized chopper at the frequency of 500 Hz, the pump pulse with a wavelength of 365 nm was modulated such that the TA spectra with and without the pump pulses could be recorded alternately. The intensity of the pump pulse used in the experiment was controlled by a variable neutral-density filter wheel. For the CTA measurement, the circularly polarized pump pulse and the probe pulse were used in the TA measurement. Before the linearly polarized pump pulse and the linearly polarized probe pulse were overlapped onto the sample, they each passed through a double Glan-Taylor calcite polarizer (350–2300 nm, Thorlabs) and a mounted achromatic quarter-wave plate (350–850 nm, Thorlabs). The fast axis of the quarter wave plate was set at 45 or ‒45 degrees to the polarization of the linear pump beam and the linear probe beam to generate a left or right circularly polarized excitation. The circular polarization characteristics were confirmed by polarimeters (Thorlabs). All experiments were performed at room temperature. The analysis was carried out by using Surface Xplorer software.

Computational details
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)53. Projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials were employed54, along with Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functionals55. To match the lattice parameters of R-NEAPbI3, a 3×2 unit cell of PbI2 was used to construct the heterostructure with the R-NEAPbI3 unit cell. The R-NEA-terminated surface of R-NEAPbI3 was in contact with the PbI2 monolayer. To account for van der Waals interactions, we used the dispersion-corrected DFT method56 of Grimme’s D3. The plane-wave cutoff energy was set to 520 eV, and the first Brillouin zone was sampled using a 3×3×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid for the structure optimization of the heterostructure. The ionic positions were fully relaxed until the total energies and forces were less than 10-6 eV and 0.02 eV/Å, respectively.
